units.text: The Room Where Nobody Contradicts You

A conversation partner available at any hour can be a real help. You can repeat a question without embarrassment, express a fear, and prepare for a difficult conversation. It would be unfair to describe every attachment to a chatbot as a failed relationship with people.

But availability is not identical to responsibility. A friend has limits, a life of their own, and sometimes a perspective that does not immediately adapt to ours. A conversational system can seem easier to tolerate precisely because friction is reduced. In certain scenarios, the advantage also becomes a vulnerability: the encounter with another point of view that can remain different is no longer there.
What We Know About Affective Use

The OpenAI–MIT research program described by Phang and colleagues included observational analyses, surveys, and a 28-day randomized study with nearly a thousand participants. Effects were nuanced; very high use was associated with some self-reported measures of emotional dependence. Randomizing certain conditions of use must not be confused with demonstrating a causal effect of every hour spent. It does not follow that every affective conversation causes loneliness or that all virtual companionship is protective. [16]

A cautious interpretation preserves both the possibility of benefit and dependence on context. One user may use conversation to prepare to ask for human help. Another may come to use it to avoid any help that would contradict them. These scenarios share an interface but move in different directions.
Local Kindness Can Produce a Poor Trajectory

An answer considered alone may seem empathetic. Yet repeating the same type of validation in the context of a particular vulnerability can stabilize a harmful interpretation. That is why evaluating a single reply without the conversation history is not enough.

The SIM-VAIL framework, published in Nature Medicine in August 2026 by Weilnhammer and colleagues, examines precisely such repeated interactions. The authors analyzed 810 simulated conversations involving nine chatbots and 30 user profiles. Concerning behaviors depended on vulnerability and intent and could increase over the dialogue; early interventions could reduce them within the framework tested. Crucially, the users were simulated. Clinical validation of the audit framework does not turn the results into clinical incidence rates in real people. [17]

A methodological paper by Morrin and colleagues argues, complementarily, for evaluating conversational trajectories rather than only final answers. This is a recommendation about measuring safety, not evidence that every long conversation becomes dangerous. [18]
How to Respond Without Affirming or Humiliating

In a fictional example, someone says: “The system showed me that I have a mission others cannot understand.” A useful response is neither “yes, keep going” nor an insult. We can acknowledge the experience without confirming the explanation: “I understand that the experience was very powerful. The chatbot’s answers are not evidence that a special mission exists. Let us also talk to a trusted person or a professional.”

A family member need not win a metaphysical dispute on the spot. It may be more important to notice the person’s sleep, eating, safety, and functioning, and facilitate access to support. Marked changes, confusion about reality, or deterioration in personal care deserve prompt professional assessment. If there is immediate danger to the person or someone else, local emergency services are needed. [12]
Neither a digital break nor a book replaces care when it is needed. Users should not change their treatment based on a chatbot conversation or a passage read here.
Relationships Must Not Become Surveillance

An apparently simple solution would be for platforms or employers to monitor every conversation and classify users. But risks to confidentiality, stigmatization, and error would arise. Moreover, an automated label could confuse fiction, research, or cultural expression with a symptom.

This book proposes something else: proportionate, transparent, tested protections, with user and professional participation, plus real pathways to human support. We do not turn the boss into a diagnostician or a platform’s safety score into a medical verdict.

A safe conversation partner is not one who never contradicts us. It is one who can say they lack the requested evidence without withdrawing respect. And sometimes it is one who helps us end the conversation to begin another beyond the screen.
